title: Introduction to Capital Markets
subtitle: What capital markets do, why Ethiopia built one and how ECMA, ESX and the market's institutions fit together
summary: A foundational course on Ethiopia's new capital market, following one fictional share company from private placement to listing and trading on the Ethiopian Securities Exchange.
audience: Bank, insurance and corporate staff new to capital markets, and staff of newly licensed capital market service providers such as investment banks, brokers and advisers. No prerequisites.
objectives: Explain the role of capital markets in mobilising long-term savings and financing growth
Distinguish primary and secondary markets, equity and debt, and exchange and OTC trading
Describe the institutions in the Ethiopian capital market and what each does
Trace a share company's journey from private placement to ESX listing and trading, naming the institution at each step

runningCase.name: Meskerem Agro Processing S.C.
runningCase.text: Meskerem Agro Processing S.C. is a fictional dairy and juice processor in Bishoftu, founded in 2019 as a private limited company by five founders led by managing director Tigist Alemu. It grew on bank loans and reinvested profit, and now needs Birr 600 million for a UHT milk and juice plant. Across the course it converts to a share company, raises Birr 150 million in a private placement, appoints the fictional investment bank Entoto Capital S.C., gains ECMA approval for a public offer of 2.4 million shares at Birr 250, lists on the ESX Growth Board and begins trading, with a Birr 200 million bond planned for the Fixed Income Market.

modules.title: Why capital markets matter
modules.summary: See how capital markets turn long-term savings into long-term investment, how market finance differs from bank finance, and why Ethiopia rebuilt a market after a gap of almost fifty years.
objectives: Explain how a capital market links savers who want returns with businesses and government that need long-term funds
Compare bank finance and market finance for a growing Ethiopian company
Outline Ethiopia's capital market history, from the 1960s share dealing group to the 2021 proclamation and the 2025 launch of ESX
Describe why the reform matters for banks, insurers and companies in Ethiopia

lessons.title: Savers on one side, builders on the other
body: Every economy has people and institutions with money they do not need today: households saving for retirement, insurers holding premiums, pension funds collecting contributions. It also has people who need money they do not yet have: a company building a factory, a city building roads, a government financing a dam. A financial system exists to move money from the first group to the second at a fair price.

Banks do this by taking short deposits and lending them out. A capital market does it differently: savers buy securities, such as shares and bonds, directly from the companies and governments that need funds, and can later sell those securities to other investors. The saver carries the risk and earns the return; the market supplies the price and the ability to sell.

items.label: Investors reinvest or sell to others

example.title: Two neighbours in Adama
example.text: Almaz Kebede, a teacher in Adama, has Birr 80,000 in a savings account. Her neighbour Dawit Gemechu runs a growing feed mill and needs Birr 40 million for a new line. Through the bank, Almaz's deposit may end up in a loan to Dawit, but the bank decides and takes the credit risk. Through a capital market, Almaz could buy a small piece of a company like Dawit's directly, sharing in its profits and its risks.

lessons.tip: When you hear "capital market", think "long-term money": funds committed for years, not weeks.

lessons.title: Bank finance and market finance
body: Ethiopian companies have relied almost entirely on bank loans. A loan is flexible and private, but it must be repaid on a schedule whatever happens to profits, it usually needs collateral, and banks limit how much they lend to one customer. Most bank funding is short-term deposits, so very long loans are hard for banks to offer in large amounts.

Market finance spreads the funding across many investors. Equity (shares) has no repayment date and no fixed charge: shareholders are paid from profits, if there are profits. Bonds are fixed-income borrowing from investors rather than one bank, often for longer terms. Market finance needs disclosure, a regulator's approval and more preparation, so it suits companies that are large enough and well governed.

right.title: Shares or bonds
items: Price set by investors and the market
Takes months to prepare, suits larger needs

worked.title: Meskerem's Birr 600 million plant: loan or shares? (Birr millions, illustrative)

rows.label: Funding needed for the new UHT plant
Option A: 7-year bank loan, assumed interest 17%
Option B: new shares sold to investors
Dividend if the board pays 30% of a net profit of 84

worked.note: A loan this large would leave Meskerem with almost no cushion if sales dip in year 1. Equity costs the founders a share of ownership and future profits, but it does not have to be repaid in a bad year. The interest rate is an assumption for illustration; banks now set lending rates freely.

scenario.title: Which source fits?
scenario.situation: Selamawit Haile is finance manager of a mid-sized textile exporter in Hawassa. It needs Birr 15 million for three months to buy cotton for a confirmed order, and separately plans a Birr 900 million expansion over the next four years.
scenario.question: Which pairing makes most sense?
options: Shares for the cotton and a bank overdraft for the expansion
A short bank facility for the cotton, and market finance (shares or bonds) considered for the expansion
A public share offer for both needs
Postpone the expansion until the bank offers a 20-year loan
scenario.explain: Short, self-liquidating needs suit bank facilities. A large, long-term expansion is what capital markets are for. A public offer takes months, so it cannot fund a three-month purchase, and waiting for a very long bank loan ignores the new option.

lessons.title: Five jobs a capital market does
body: A working capital market does more than raise money. It sets prices that tell investors and managers what a business is worth. It lets investors sell, which makes them more willing to commit money in the first place. It spreads risk across many holders instead of concentrating it on banks. And because listed companies must publish information, it pushes governance and transparency up across the economy.

For Ethiopia, the last job matters as much as the first. Companies that prepare for listing must keep audited accounts, hold proper shareholder meetings and disclose material news. That discipline makes them better borrowers for banks too.

items.label: Mobilise savings
items.text: Draw idle and informal savings into productive investment

items.label: Discover prices
items.text: Buyers and sellers reveal what a security is worth

items.label: Provide liquidity
items.text: Investors can sell before a bond matures or a company closes

items.label: Spread risk
items.text: Many investors share it, not only bank depositors

items.label: Raise governance
items.text: Disclosure and scrutiny improve how companies are run

example.title: The informal share market for bank shares
example.text: For years, shares of Ethiopian private banks and insurers changed hands informally: a seller found a buyer through friends, agreed a price privately and then asked the company to record the transfer. Prices were hard to discover and some sellers waited months. An organised exchange with brokers and a depository is meant to replace that slow, opaque process with visible prices and recorded trades.

lessons.title: Ethiopia's history: an early start and a long gap
body: Ethiopia is not new to share trading. In the 1960s an informal share dealing group in Addis Ababa brought together buyers and sellers of company shares and some government bonds. That activity ended in the 1970s when private enterprises were nationalised, and for close to fifty years the country had no organised securities market.

Private banks and insurers reappeared from the 1990s and sold shares to thousands of Ethiopians, but those shares had nowhere organised to trade. The turning point came with the Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021, which created the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority (ECMA). ECMA then issued directives on licensing, fees, exchanges and public offers, and the Ethiopian Securities Exchange (ESX) launched on 10 January 2025.

items.label: 1960s
items.text: An informal share dealing group operates in Addis Ababa

items.label: 1970s
items.text: Nationalisation ends private share trading

items.label: 1990s onward
items.text: Private banks and insurers raise capital from many shareholders, trading stays informal
Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021 creates ECMA
ECMA licensing, fee, exchange and public offer directives; ESX Rulebook in December

items.label: 10 January 2025
items.text: The Ethiopian Securities Exchange launches

regulation.text: The proclamation created Ethiopia's capital market framework and established the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority as regulator. It covers securities exchanges, licensing of capital market service providers, public offers and market abuse, and it gives ECMA the power to issue directives. It was adopted as part of the Homegrown Economic Reform programme and the Ten Year Development Plan.

lessons.tip: When a colleague says Ethiopia has "no experience" of capital markets, remember the 1960s: the gap was long, but the idea is not foreign.

lessons.title: Why Ethiopia built a market now
body: The Ten Year Development Plan and the Homegrown Economic Reform programme set ambitious goals for private-sector growth, manufacturing and infrastructure. Those goals need long-term finance on a scale that bank deposits alone cannot supply. A capital market gives companies another source and gives the government a deeper market for its own securities.

The timing also fits wider reforms: a market-based exchange rate regime from 2024, an interest-rate-based monetary policy framework, and the opening of banking to foreign banks. Together these make prices, including interest rates and share prices, more meaningful signals than before.
points: Companies gain a source of long-term equity and debt beyond bank loans
Savers gain investments other than deposits, land, buildings and gold
The government gains a deeper, more transparent market for its debt
Banks gain new business lines in brokerage, advice, custody and asset management

scenario.title: A board member's question
scenario.situation: At a board meeting of a regional insurer, director Tesfaye Mulatu asks: "We already invest in bank deposits and buildings. Why should we care about the new exchange?" The insurer holds Birr 2 billion of policyholder funds, most of it in deposits.
scenario.question: Which answer best explains the relevance?
options: The market offers long-term assets such as bonds and listed shares that can be valued daily and sold if needed, which can match long-term liabilities better than deposits
It does not matter, because insurers may only hold deposits
The exchange matters only for companies that want to list
The exchange guarantees higher returns than deposits
scenario.explain: Insurers and pension funds have long-term liabilities and benefit from long-term, tradeable assets. No exchange guarantees returns, and listing is only one side of the market; investors are the other.

lessons.title: Meet the running case: Meskerem Agro Processing S.C.
body: Throughout this course you will follow Meskerem Agro Processing S.C., a fictional dairy and juice processor in Bishoftu. It began in 2019 as a private limited company owned by five founders and grew on bank loans and reinvested profit. It now wants to build a Birr 600 million UHT milk and juice plant, more than its banks can lend and more than its founders can contribute.

In each module Meskerem takes one more step: deciding to raise market finance, choosing instruments, appointing advisers and dealing with ECMA, listing on ESX and, finally, meeting the investors who trade its shares. At every step, ask yourself which institution is involved and what it does.

example.title: The founders' dilemma
example.text: Tigist Alemu, Meskerem's managing director and largest founder, owns 40% of the company. If Meskerem sells new shares equal to 30% of the enlarged company, her stake falls to 28%. She keeps control of the board with her co-founders, and owns a smaller share of a much larger company. Every founder who considers a listing faces this trade-off.

lessons.tip: Keep a one-page "Meskerem map" as you study: each step, the institution involved and the document it produces.

takeaways: Capital markets move long-term savings into long-term investment through securities such as shares and bonds
Bank finance suits short, routine needs; market finance suits large, long-term needs of well governed companies
Markets mobilise savings, discover prices, provide liquidity, spread risk and raise governance standards
Ethiopia had an informal share dealing group in the 1960s, a long gap after nationalisation, then the 2021 proclamation and the ESX launch on 10 January 2025
The market supports the Ten Year Development Plan and the Homegrown Economic Reform programme

quiz.q: What is the main difference between how a bank and a capital market channel savings?
options: Banks only serve companies, markets only serve government
In a market, savers buy securities directly and carry the issuer's risk; in a bank, the bank lends and carries the credit risk
Banks are regulated and markets are not
quiz.explain: In market finance the investor holds the security and its risk; in bank finance the bank stands between saver and borrower.

quiz.q: Which need is best suited to a capital market rather than a bank overdraft?
options: A Birr 600 million plant to be repaid from profits over many years
A three-month purchase of raw materials
quiz.explain: Capital markets specialise in large, long-term funding.

quiz.q: Which law created the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority?
options: National Bank of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 1359/2025
quiz.explain: Proclamation No. 1248/2021 established ECMA and the capital market framework.

quiz.q: When did the Ethiopian Securities Exchange launch?
quiz.explain: ESX launched on 10 January 2025, after the Rulebook was issued in December 2024.

quiz.q: What happened to Ethiopia's 1960s share dealing activity?
options: It became today's ESX without a break
It ended when private enterprises were nationalised in the 1970s
quiz.explain: Nationalisation in the 1970s ended private share trading, leaving a gap of about fifty years.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the jobs a capital market does?
quiz.explain: Markets offer opportunity and liquidity, not guaranteed returns.

modules.title: How the market is structured
modules.summary: Separate primary from secondary markets, money markets from capital markets and exchange from OTC trading, and see how the ESX Main Board, Growth Board and Fixed Income Market fit together.
objectives: Distinguish primary and secondary markets and explain why each needs the other
Distinguish the money market from the capital market by maturity and purpose
Explain the difference between exchange trading and over-the-counter (OTC) trading in Ethiopia
Describe the three ESX markets and the basic trading rules in the ESX Rulebook

lessons.title: Primary and secondary markets
body: The primary market is where securities are created and sold for the first time. When Meskerem sells new shares to investors, the money goes to Meskerem and is used to build the plant. A government Treasury bill auction is also a primary market: the money goes to the government.

The secondary market is where investors trade existing securities among themselves. When an investor later sells Meskerem shares on ESX, the money goes to the selling investor, not to Meskerem. The secondary market raises no new money for the company, but without it few investors would buy in the primary market, because they could never get their money out.

left.title: Primary market
items: Examples: share offer, T-bill auction, bond issue

right.title: Secondary market
items: Money goes to the selling investor
Prices move with supply and demand
Example: trading listed shares on ESX

scenario.title: Where does the money go?
scenario.situation: Mekdes Tadesse bought 500 Meskerem shares in the public offer at Birr 250 each. A year later she sells them on ESX to Yonas Girma at Birr 290 each.
scenario.question: Who receives the Birr 145,000 that Yonas pays, before fees?
options: Mekdes, because this is a secondary market trade
Meskerem, because they are its shares
ECMA, which holds it until the next offer
scenario.explain: In a secondary trade the seller receives the proceeds. Meskerem received money only once, in the primary offer. ECMA regulates, and brokers earn a commission, not the trade value.

lessons.title: Money market and capital market
body: Financial markets are also split by maturity. The money market deals in short-term instruments, usually one year or less, such as Treasury bills and interbank lending. Banks and companies use it to manage liquidity: parking surplus cash for weeks or borrowing to cover a short gap.

The capital market deals in long-term instruments: shares, which never mature, and bonds that run for several years. It finances investment rather than day-to-day liquidity. In Ethiopia the NBE runs the Treasury bill market on behalf of government and sets the policy rate that anchors money market rates, while ECMA regulates securities and the capital market.

left.title: Money market
items: Maturity of one year or less
Anchored by the NBE policy rate

right.title: Capital market
items: Maturity above one year, or none for shares

example.title: A treasury desk's week
example.text: Kidist Abebe works on the treasury desk of a commercial bank in Addis Ababa. On Monday she bids in the NBE Treasury bill auction to place surplus liquidity for 91 days. On Wednesday she lends to another bank overnight. Both are money market activities. Her colleague in the investment unit, meanwhile, studies a five-year bond listed on the ESX Fixed Income Market: that is the capital market.

lessons.title: Exchange trading and OTC trading
body: On an exchange, orders from many buyers and sellers meet in one central order book under the exchange's rules, and prices are visible to all members. Securities must be listed, and listed companies follow continuing disclosure rules. ESX is Ethiopia's securities exchange.

Over-the-counter (OTC) trading happens directly between two parties, usually through a licensed dealer, outside the central order book. OTC markets suit securities that are not listed or that trade rarely. In Ethiopia the OTC market sits under ECMA's directive on securities exchanges, derivatives exchanges and the OTC market (reported as Directive No. 1009/2024), not under the ESX Rulebook. This matters for the many unlisted share companies whose shareholders still want a way to trade.

left.title: Exchange (ESX)
items: Governed by the ESX Rulebook and ECMA directives

right.title: OTC market
items: Governed by ECMA's exchanges and OTC directive

regulation.source: ECMA directive on securities exchanges, derivatives exchanges and the OTC market (reported as Directive No. 1009/2024)
regulation.text: ECMA licenses and supervises securities exchanges, derivatives exchanges and the OTC market under one directive, issued under the Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021. The ESX Rulebook governs trading on ESX itself; the OTC market is governed by the ECMA directive, not by the Rulebook.

lessons.tip: Ask two questions about any trade: is the security listed, and did the order go to the exchange's order book? If not, it is OTC.

lessons.title: The three ESX markets
body: The ESX Rulebook of December 2024 sets up three markets. The Main Board is for larger, established companies that meet the full listing requirements. The Growth Board is for smaller or younger companies with growth potential, with requirements suited to their size. The Fixed Income Market lists bonds and other debt securities, including government and corporate bonds.

Each market has its own listing rules, and the company and its advisers decide which market fits. The Rulebook also sets membership categories for the firms allowed to trade on ESX, so investors always reach the exchange through a member such as a licensed broker.

items.label: Main Board
items.text: Established, larger companies meeting the full listing rules

items.label: Growth Board
items.text: Smaller and younger companies with growth potential

items.label: Fixed Income Market
items.text: Government and corporate bonds and other debt securities

example.title: Choosing a board for Meskerem
example.text: Meskerem's adviser, the fictional Entoto Capital S.C., compares Meskerem's age, size, profit record and governance with the listing rules of each market. Meskerem has a strong but short track record, so Entoto recommends the Growth Board for its shares now. Later, Meskerem plans a corporate bond, which would list on the Fixed Income Market.

scenario.title: Matching issuers to ESX markets
scenario.situation: Three fictional issuers approach ESX: Rift Valley Solar S.C., a four-year-old solar installer growing fast; Abuna Cement S.C., a large cement maker profitable for fifteen years; and Sheger Housing S.C., which wants to issue a seven-year bond.
scenario.question: Which match is most sensible, subject to each meeting the actual listing rules?
options: Rift Valley Solar: Main Board; Abuna Cement: Fixed Income Market; Sheger Housing: Growth Board
All three on the Main Board
Rift Valley Solar: Growth Board; Abuna Cement: Main Board; Sheger Housing bond: Fixed Income Market
All three on the OTC market
scenario.explain: The Growth Board suits younger, fast-growing companies, the Main Board established ones, and the Fixed Income Market debt securities. Listing still depends on meeting the Rulebook criteria for each.

lessons.title: A trading day on ESX
body: The ESX Rulebook sets trading from 9:00 to 15:00, with a 30-minute pre-open session in which orders are entered before continuous trading begins. The lot size is one share, so a retail investor can buy even a single share; there is no minimum block.

Some details that investors often ask about, such as the settlement cycle, tick size and daily price limits, are not stated in the Rulebook. They depend on central securities depository rules and ESX notices, so always check the latest notice rather than assuming a number from another country's exchange.

items.label: Pre-open
items.text: 30 minutes before continuous trading: orders are entered

items.label: Opening
items.text: Continuous trading begins

items.label: Trading 9:00 to 15:00
items.text: Buy and sell orders are matched in the order book

items.label: Close
items.text: Trading stops and the day's prices are published

items.label: Post-trade
items.text: Clearing and settlement under depository rules

regulation.text: The Rulebook establishes the Main Board, Growth Board and Fixed Income Market, sets membership categories, and sets trading from 9:00 to 15:00 with a 30-minute pre-open and a lot size of one share. It does not state a settlement cycle, tick size or price limits.

rows.label: Order: buy 1,000 Meskerem shares at Birr 250
ECMA transaction fee on shares, 0.15% (Directive No. 996/2024)
Broker commission, assumed 0.5% (set by the broker)
