takeaways: The primary market raises new money for issuers; the secondary market lets investors trade and so makes them willing to buy in the first place
The money market handles short-term liquidity, the capital market long-term investment
Exchange trades go through a central order book; OTC trades are bilateral, and in Ethiopia the OTC market sits under ECMA's exchanges and OTC directive, not the ESX Rulebook
ESX has a Main Board, a Growth Board and a Fixed Income Market
ESX trades from 9:00 to 15:00 after a 30-minute pre-open, with a lot size of one share

quiz.q: A government Treasury bill auction is an example of:
options: A primary market in the money market
quiz.explain: The bills are newly issued and short-term, so it is a primary money market transaction.

quiz.q: When shares are sold on ESX from one investor to another, the issuing company:
quiz.explain: Secondary trades transfer money between investors only.

quiz.q: Which ESX market would normally list a corporate bond?
quiz.explain: The Fixed Income Market is ESX's market for debt securities.

quiz.q: Under which instrument does Ethiopia's OTC market sit?
options: ECMA's directive on exchanges, derivatives exchanges and the OTC market
quiz.explain: The OTC market is governed by the ECMA directive, not by the ESX Rulebook.

quiz.q: What is the lot size for shares under the ESX Rulebook?
quiz.explain: The Rulebook sets a lot size of one share.

quiz.q: Which item is NOT stated in the ESX Rulebook?
quiz.explain: The Rulebook sets no settlement cycle, tick size or price limits.

modules.title: The instruments investors buy
modules.summary: Understand shares, government and corporate bonds, Treasury bills, collective investment schemes and future derivatives: what each pays, what can go wrong and who uses it.
objectives: Explain what a share gives its holder and how shareholders earn a return
Compare government bonds, corporate bonds and Treasury bills by issuer, maturity and risk
Calculate a dividend yield, a bond coupon and a Treasury bill price
Describe collective investment schemes and why derivatives are still a future step in Ethiopia

lessons.title: Shares: owning part of a company
body: A share is a unit of ownership in a share company. Ordinary shareholders vote at the general meeting, elect the board and share in profits through dividends declared by the company. They are paid last if the company fails, after creditors, so they carry the most risk and expect the highest long-term return.

A shareholder earns in two ways: dividends, and a rise in the share price when the company grows. Neither is guaranteed. Under the Commercial Code of 2021, only a share company can offer shares to the public, which is why many Ethiopian private limited companies must convert before they can list.

worked.title: Return on a Meskerem share over one year (illustrative)

rows.label: Price paid at the start of the year
Price at the end of the year
Total return before costs and tax

worked.note: In a different year the price could fall and the dividend could be cut, giving a negative return. Investors compare this risk with safer options such as T-bills.

example.title: Founders' shares and new shares
example.text: Before its offer, Meskerem has 5.6 million shares held by founders and private placement investors. It plans to issue 2.4 million new shares, so after the offer 8 million shares exist and the new investors hold 30%. Each new share carries the same voting and dividend rights as the founders' shares.

lessons.title: Treasury bills and government bonds
body: The government borrows through Treasury bills, which mature in one year or less, and government bonds, which run longer. The Ministry of Finance is the issuer and the NBE runs the T-bill auctions. Because the government taxes and borrows in Birr, its Birr securities are treated as the lowest-risk Birr asset, so their yields act as a benchmark for other rates.

A T-bill pays no coupon. It is sold at a discount and repaid at face value: the investor's return is the difference. As reported in the NBE's July 2026 Monetary Policy Committee release, the 91-day T-bill yield was 11.0%. Rates change at every auction, so always use the latest figure.

worked.title: Price of a 91-day T-bill at an 11.0% yield
worked.note: This uses a simple 365-day yield formula for teaching. Auction conventions can differ, so check the NBE auction notice for the exact basis.

regulation.source: National Bank of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 1359/2025, Art. 27
regulation.text: The NBE may lend to government through an overdraft of at most 12 months and 15% of average government revenue, and it may not buy government securities in the primary market. Government must therefore sell its bills and bonds to banks, institutions and other investors, which is one reason a deeper government securities market matters.

scenario.title: Parking a pension fund's cash
scenario.situation: The fictional Kombolcha Employees' Provident Fund will pay Birr 30 million of retirement benefits in exactly three months. Its trustee, Hailu Bekele, can choose between a 91-day T-bill, listed shares and a five-year corporate bond.
scenario.question: Which is the best home for this money?
options: Listed shares, because they may rise most
The 91-day T-bill, which matures when the money is needed and carries government credit
The five-year corporate bond, for its higher coupon
scenario.explain: Money needed in three months should be in a short, low-risk instrument that matures on time. Shares and a long bond could be worth less when the payment falls due, and idle cash earns nothing.

lessons.title: Corporate bonds
body: A corporate bond is a loan from investors to a company. The company promises a fixed or floating coupon, paid usually once or twice a year, and repays the face value at maturity. Bondholders do not vote and do not share in extra profit, but they are paid before shareholders and their income is set in advance.

Because a company can fail, corporate bonds pay more than government securities of the same term. The extra yield, called the credit spread, compensates for that risk. Credit rating agencies, once licensed in Ethiopia, will help investors judge the spread by grading the issuer.

worked.title: Meskerem's planned bond (illustrative)

rows.label: Term and coupon
rows.value: 5 years, 15% a year, paid twice a year

rows.label: Coupon every six months (200 m x 15% / 2)

worked.note: Meskerem must budget Birr 30 million of coupons each year whatever its profit, which is why it raises equity first and keeps the bond smaller.

lessons.title: Collective investment schemes
body: A collective investment scheme, such as a unit trust or mutual fund, pools money from many investors and has a licensed fund manager invest it in a spread of securities. Each investor owns units in the fund rather than the securities directly. This gives a small saver diversification and professional management that would be hard to achieve alone.

The fund's assets are held by an independent custodian, not by the manager, to protect investors. ECMA regulates these schemes through a directive on collective investment schemes. The investor pays management fees, and the value of units rises and falls with the fund's holdings.

items.label: Investors buy units
items.text: Many small amounts are pooled

items.label: Fund manager invests
items.text: In T-bills, bonds and listed shares under the fund's rules

items.label: Custodian holds assets
items.text: Separate from the manager's own money

items.label: Value is published
items.text: Units are priced from the value of the holdings

items.label: Investors redeem or hold
items.text: Sell units back or keep them for the long term

example.title: A nurse's first fund
example.text: Hiwot Desta, a nurse in Dire Dawa, can save Birr 3,000 a month. Buying a spread of shares and bonds with that amount would be costly and slow. By buying units in a fictional balanced fund managed by Tana Asset Management S.C., she owns a small slice of a portfolio of T-bills, bonds and listed shares, with a custodian holding the assets.

lessons.title: Derivatives: a future step
body: A derivative is a contract whose value depends on another asset, such as a share, a bond, a currency or a commodity. Futures, options and swaps let users hedge risks, for example locking in a coffee price or an exchange rate. They can also magnify losses when used to speculate.

Ethiopia's framework already provides for derivatives exchanges to be licensed by ECMA, but an exchange-traded derivatives market is a later stage of development. Do not confuse derivatives with the Ethiopia Commodity Exchange (ECX), which trades physical commodities such as coffee, sesame and pulses. Forward foreign exchange contracts offered by banks under NBE rules are a separate, bank-based product.

scenario.title: A client asks about futures
scenario.situation: A coffee exporter, Abdi Mohammed, asks his bank relationship manager whether he can buy coffee futures on ESX to lock in next season's price.
scenario.question: What is the most accurate reply?
options: Yes, ESX lists coffee futures on its Growth Board
Coffee futures trade on the Fixed Income Market
Derivatives are banned in Ethiopia forever
The framework allows derivatives exchanges to be licensed, but exchange-traded derivatives are not yet a developed market; ECX trades physical coffee, and price hedging needs other tools for now
scenario.explain: ESX lists shares and debt securities, not commodity futures. Derivatives are provided for in the framework as a future step, and ECX is a physical commodity exchange. Saying they are banned forever is wrong.

takeaways: Shares give ownership, votes and a residual claim on profits; returns come from dividends and price changes
Treasury bills mature in a year or less, are sold at a discount and set the benchmark for Birr rates
Corporate bonds pay a promised coupon and rank ahead of shares, with a credit spread over government yields
Collective investment schemes pool small savings under a licensed manager with an independent custodian
Derivatives are a future step; ECX trades physical commodities and is not a derivatives market

quiz.q: A share bought at Birr 200 pays a Birr 12 dividend. What is the dividend yield?
A Treasury bill earns its return by:
options: Being sold at a discount and repaid at face value
quiz.explain: T-bills are discount instruments with no coupon.

quiz.q: Who ranks first if a company is wound up?
options: Unit holders of a fund that owns its shares
quiz.explain: Creditors, including bondholders, are paid before shareholders.

quiz.q: A Birr 50 million bond pays 14% a year, twice a year. What is each coupon payment?
quiz.explain: 50 million x 14% / 2 = Birr 3.5 million.

quiz.q: In a collective investment scheme, who holds the fund's assets?
quiz.explain: A custodian holds the assets separately to protect investors.

quiz.q: What does the Ethiopia Commodity Exchange (ECX) trade?
options: Physical commodities such as coffee and sesame
quiz.explain: ECX trades physical commodities; it is separate from ESX.

modules.title: The institutions and who does what
modules.summary: Meet ECMA, ESX, the central securities depository and the licensed service providers, and see how the NBE and the Ministry of Finance fit in, by following Meskerem from private placement to its first trade.
objectives: Describe the roles of ECMA, ESX and the central securities depository
Explain what investment banks, brokers, dealers, investment advisers, fund managers, custodians and credit rating agencies do
Explain the roles of the NBE and the Ministry of Finance in the capital market
Name the institution involved at each step of a company's journey from private placement to trading

lessons.title: The regulator, the exchange and the depository
body: Three institutions form the core of the market. ECMA is the regulator: it licenses exchanges and service providers, approves public offers, writes directives, supervises conduct and acts against market abuse. ESX is the exchange: it admits securities to its markets, admits members, runs the trading system and enforces its Rulebook on listed companies and members.

The central securities depository (CSD) holds securities in electronic form and records who owns what. When a trade on ESX is completed, the CSD moves the shares from seller to buyer in its records. Dematerialisation, replacing paper share certificates with electronic records, is what makes fast, safe transfers possible.

items.label: ECMA
items.text: Regulator: licenses, approves offers, supervises, enforces

items.label: ESX
items.text: Exchange: listings, members, trading and market rules

items.label: CSD
items.text: Depository: electronic records of ownership and settlement of trades

example.title: From certificates to records
example.text: Meskerem's founders held paper share certificates kept in a safe at the company office, and the company secretary updated a handwritten share register. Before listing, Meskerem's shares are dematerialised: each holder opens an account through a licensed intermediary, and the CSD records their holdings electronically. The paper certificates are cancelled.

lessons.title: Licensed capital market service providers
body: No investor deals with ESX directly. Firms licensed by ECMA stand between investors, issuers and the market. Investment banks advise companies on raising capital, prepare offers and may underwrite them. Brokers execute client orders on the exchange for a commission; dealers trade on their own account and can quote prices. Investment advisers give investment advice, fund managers run portfolios and collective schemes, and custodians hold assets safely for clients.

Credit rating agencies grade the creditworthiness of bond issuers, which helps investors price corporate bonds. Each type of firm needs its own licence, its own minimum capital and fit and proper management.

items.label: Investment bank
items.text: Advises issuers, structures and underwrites offers

items.label: Broker
items.text: Executes client orders on ESX for a commission

items.label: Dealer
items.text: Buys and sells on its own account, quotes prices

items.label: Investment adviser
items.text: Gives advice suited to the client's needs

items.label: Fund manager
items.text: Manages portfolios and collective schemes

items.label: Custodian
items.text: Holds clients' securities and cash safely

items.label: Credit rating agency
items.text: Grades issuers' ability to repay debt

regulation.source: ECMA Directive No. 980/2024, licensing and supervision of capital market service providers
regulation.text: The directive sets 15 licence categories for capital market service providers. Minimum capital ranges from Birr 100,000 for an individual investment adviser to Birr 100 million for an investment bank in a bank group or a custodian. Licensed firms must keep 40% of their minimum capital in liquid assets and renew their licence every year.

worked.title: ECMA fees for a new broker (Directive No. 996/2024)

rows.label: Annual renewal fee from the second year
Fees over the first three years (192,000 + 2 x 66,000)

worked.note: Fees are only part of the cost: the firm must also meet minimum capital under Directive No. 980/2024, hire qualified staff and build systems. The fee schedule can change, so check the current directive.

lessons.title: The roles of the NBE and the Ministry of Finance
body: The NBE is not the capital market regulator, but it shapes the market in three ways. It sets monetary policy through the National Bank Rate, which drives yields on T-bills and bonds. It runs the government securities auctions. And it regulates banks, including how much banks may invest in shares and in capital market subsidiaries.

The Ministry of Finance issues government securities and manages public debt. The size and pricing of its borrowing affect how much money is left for private issuers and what return investors demand. Because both bodies affect the market, ECMA, the NBE and the Ministry of Finance coordinate on government securities and on the role of banks.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/92/2024, limits on bank investments
regulation.text: The directive limits bank investments to 5% in a single insurer, 10% in any other single non-bank business, 15% of total capital for all non-bank equity together, and 10% in real estate. With NBE approval, a bank may own up to 100% of a capital market service provider, which is how many banks are setting up investment bank and brokerage subsidiaries.

scenario.title: Who regulates what?
scenario.situation: A bank plans a brokerage subsidiary. Its strategy officer, Meron Assefa, drafts a plan saying "ECMA will approve the bank's investment in the subsidiary, and the NBE will license the broker."
scenario.question: What correction should she make?
options: Reverse it: the NBE approves the bank's investment under SBB/92/2024, and ECMA licenses the brokerage under Directive No. 980/2024
The Ministry of Finance approves both
scenario.explain: Bank investments are an NBE prudential matter; licensing of capital market service providers is ECMA's job. ESX admits members but does not license firms, and the Ministry of Finance is an issuer.

lessons.title: Meskerem's journey, step by step
body: Here is the full life of the running case, with the institution at each step. In 2023 Meskerem converts from a private limited company into a share company, registered under the Commercial Code. In 2024 it raises Birr 150 million through a private placement to 35 selected investors, including a private insurer and diaspora investors, without a public prospectus.

In 2025 Meskerem appoints Entoto Capital S.C., a licensed investment bank, as transaction adviser and lead arranger. Entoto and Meskerem's auditors prepare a prospectus with audited accounts, which ECMA reviews and approves. The shares are dematerialised at the CSD, ESX approves the listing on the Growth Board, and licensed brokers such as the fictional Sheba Securities S.C. take investors' applications. In 2026 Meskerem raises Birr 600 million and its shares begin trading.

items.label: Convert to a share company
items.text: Commercial Code; trade registration

items.label: Private placement
items.text: Selected investors, within ECMA's private placement limits

items.label: Appoint advisers
items.text: Investment bank, auditors and legal adviser

items.label: Prospectus approved
items.text: ECMA reviews and approves the public offer

items.label: Dematerialise shares
items.text: CSD records holdings electronically

items.label: Offer and listing
items.text: Brokers collect applications; ESX admits the shares

items.label: Trading
items.text: Brokers trade on ESX; CSD settles; ECMA supervises

worked.title: ECMA fee on Meskerem's public share offer (Directive No. 996/2024)

rows.label: Fixed fee for a share offer

worked.note: The ECMA fee is about 0.15% of the money raised. Adviser, underwriting, legal, audit and marketing costs are usually much larger, so issuers budget for the whole cost of the offer, not only the regulator's fee.

lessons.title: What an underwriter does
body: In a public offer, the issuer wants certainty that it will raise the money. An investment bank can underwrite the offer: it commits to buy any shares the public does not take, at an agreed price, in exchange for a fee. If the offer is fully taken up, the underwriter keeps its fee and buys nothing; if it is undersubscribed, the underwriter must pay for the rest.

Underwriting shifts the risk of a failed offer from the issuer to the investment bank, so the bank must have capital to back it. This is one reason the minimum capital for an investment bank is far higher than for an adviser.

example.title: An undersubscribed offer
example.text: A fictional cement company, Abuna Cement S.C., offers Birr 400 million of new shares, fully underwritten by Entoto Capital. The public applies for only Birr 340 million. Entoto must buy the remaining Birr 60 million of shares at the offer price and then sell them over time. Abuna still receives the full Birr 400 million.

scenario.title: Choosing the right firm
scenario.situation: Meskerem's shareholder, Kebede Worku, wants to sell 2,000 of his shares after listing. He calls the company secretary to ask how.
scenario.question: Whom should the company secretary refer him to?
options: ECMA, which buys shares from investors
Meskerem's own finance department, which will buy them back
A licensed broker who is an ESX member, who will place his sell order on ESX
scenario.explain: Investors reach the exchange through licensed broker members. ECMA regulates but does not trade, rating agencies grade debt issuers, and the company does not run its own share market.

takeaways: ECMA regulates, ESX runs the exchange, and the CSD holds electronic records of ownership and settles trades
Investment banks, brokers, dealers, advisers, fund managers, custodians and rating agencies each need their own ECMA licence under Directive No. 980/2024
The NBE shapes the market through monetary policy, T-bill auctions and bank investment limits; the Ministry of Finance issues government securities
Every step of a listing involves a named institution, from Commercial Code conversion to CSD dematerialisation and ESX admission
Underwriters take the risk of an undersubscribed offer, which is why investment banks need substantial capital

quiz.q: Which institution approves a company's public offer prospectus?
quiz.explain: ECMA reviews and approves public offers.

quiz.q: What does the central securities depository do?
options: Records ownership of securities electronically and transfers them when trades settle
quiz.explain: The CSD keeps the electronic register and settles transfers.

quiz.q: Which firm trades securities on its own account and can quote buy and sell prices?
quiz.explain: Dealers act as principal; brokers act for clients.

quiz.q: Under SBB/92/2024, a bank may own up to what share of a capital market service provider, with NBE approval?
quiz.explain: With NBE approval a bank may own all of a capital market service provider.

quiz.q: Under Directive No. 980/2024, how much of its minimum capital must a licensed firm keep in liquid assets?
quiz.explain: The directive requires 40% of minimum capital in liquid assets.

quiz.q: If an underwritten offer is undersubscribed, who buys the unsold shares?
options: Nobody; the issuer receives less money
quiz.explain: The underwriter commits to take up unsold shares at the offer price.

modules.title: Investors and the Ethiopian market today
modules.summary: Understand who invests and what each may buy, read the first steps of the Ethiopian market, and complete Meskerem's journey from listing to everyday trading.
objectives: Describe retail, diaspora, institutional and foreign investors and what shapes their choices
Explain how inflation and interest rates affect the real return investors earn
Describe the state of the Ethiopian market: first listings, unlisted share companies, the Ethio telecom share sale and the pipeline of bank listings
Trace a share company's full journey and name the institution at each step

lessons.title: Who invests
body: Retail investors are individuals buying with their own savings, often for the first time. Diaspora investors are Ethiopians and people of Ethiopian origin living abroad, who can bring foreign currency savings home. Institutional investors, such as pension funds, insurers and banks, manage large pools of money on behalf of others and usually invest for the long term.

Foreign investors are the newest group. ECMA posted a draft Foreign Portfolio Investment Regulation for consultation on 29 September 2026; once adopted, it is expected to set the terms on which foreign investors may buy listed Ethiopian securities. Until then, check the rules in force before advising any foreign client.

items.label: Retail
items.text: Individuals; need clear information and protection

items.label: Diaspora
items.text: Ethiopians abroad; bring savings and foreign currency

items.label: Pension funds and insurers
items.text: Long-term liabilities, need long-term assets

items.label: Banks
items.text: Invest within NBE limits; set up capital market subsidiaries

items.label: Foreign investors
items.text: Terms expected under the draft portfolio investment regulation

example.title: A diaspora investor in Washington
example.text: Elsa Gebremariam, an engineer in Washington, wants to invest in Ethiopian companies she knows. She opens an account with a licensed Ethiopian broker, completes the identity checks and funds it through a bank. Her holdings sit in the CSD under her account, held for her by a custodian. She applies for Meskerem shares in the public offer.

lessons.title: What investors weigh: return, risk, liquidity and inflation
body: Every investor balances return, risk and liquidity. A T-bill is low-risk and short but yields less; shares can earn more but can fall; a thinly traded share may be hard to sell quickly. Investors also look at the real return: the return after inflation, because that is what preserves buying power.

Monetary policy moves all of these. When the NBE raises the National Bank Rate, T-bill and deposit yields tend to rise, making fixed income more attractive and putting pressure on share prices. Exchange rate reform matters too: a weaker Birr raises import costs for companies like Meskerem, which imports packaging, and affects what diaspora investors earn in their home currency.

visual.caption: Figures as reported in the NBE Monetary Policy Committee release No. 7 (13 July 2026). Update them from the latest release before use.

worked.title: Real return on a 91-day T-bill (rates as reported in July 2026)
worked.note: At these rates a T-bill holder loses buying power, which is why some savers look at shares for long-term growth. Shares carry more risk, and real returns change as inflation and yields move.

scenario.title: Advising a cautious retiree
scenario.situation: Ato Getachew Lemma, 66, has Birr 1.2 million from selling a house. He needs about Birr 10,000 a month for living costs and has heard friends made money on new listings. He asks you to put everything into one newly listed share.
scenario.question: What is the most appropriate response for a licensed adviser?
options: Do as he asks, because it is his money
Tell him shares are always better than T-bills
Explain the risk of putting everything in one share, and suggest a mix that keeps living costs in short, low-risk instruments with only a part in diversified shares or a fund
scenario.explain: Advice must suit the client's needs and risk. A retiree who depends on the money needs liquidity and safety first; concentrating in one new share risks his living costs. No investment is always better, and refusing service is not the answer.

lessons.title: Public offers, private placements and investor protection
body: The difference between a private placement and a public offer is about who is protected. A private placement goes to a limited number of selected investors who can assess the company themselves, so it needs less formal disclosure. A public offer reaches anyone, so it requires an approved prospectus that sets out the business, the risks, the use of proceeds and audited accounts.

Investor protection continues after listing. Listed companies must publish results and material news promptly, insiders may not trade on information the market does not have, and ECMA can act against market manipulation. For retail investors new to the market, reading the prospectus and the company's announcements is the first defence.

regulation.source: ECMA directive on public offer and trading of securities (reported as Directive No. 1030/2024)
regulation.text: The directive governs public offers, prospectus approval and registration of securities, and the trading of securities. As reported, a private placement may be made to no more than 100 investors; an offer to more people is a public offer that needs an approved prospectus. Check the official text before relying on the figure.

scenario.title: Private placement or public offer?
scenario.situation: Rift Valley Solar S.C. wants to raise Birr 80 million by inviting 450 employees, customers and local residents to buy shares through a WhatsApp group, without a prospectus. Its CEO, Natnael Tesfaye, says this is "just a private placement".
scenario.question: What should the company's adviser say?
options: Agree, because the investors are friendly
An invitation to 450 people is well beyond the reported private placement limit, so it is a public offer that needs ECMA's prospectus approval
It is fine as long as the shares are not listed
Only the NBE can decide this
scenario.explain: Offering to hundreds of people is public by nature and needs an approved prospectus. Calling it private does not change the rule, listing is a separate question, and ECMA, not the NBE, regulates offers.

lessons.title: The Ethiopian market today
body: ESX opened in January 2025 with a small number of listings and has been adding issuers and members step by step. Its biggest untapped pool is the large base of unlisted share companies, above all private banks and insurers with thousands of shareholders who until now traded only informally. Many of these companies are preparing to list, and banks raising capital to meet the NBE's higher minimum capital requirement add to the pipeline.

The Ethio telecom share sale, in which the state telecom operator offered a minority stake to Ethiopian investors, brought many first-time investors into the market and showed the public appetite for shares. Liquidity, the ease of buying and selling, is still low, as in most young markets. Building it will take more listings, more licensed brokers, institutional investors and, in time, foreign portfolio investors.
points: Opportunity: a deep pipeline of established share companies, especially banks and insurers
Opportunity: retail interest shown by the Ethio telecom share sale
Constraint: low trading volumes and few market makers so far
Constraint: limited investor education and research coverage
Constraint: foreign portfolio rules still in draft as of late 2026

example.title: A bank's shareholders move onto the exchange
example.text: A fictional private bank, Bank A, has 9,000 shareholders who bought shares over twenty years. Before listing, a shareholder who wanted to sell had to find a buyer privately and wait for the board to record the transfer. After Bank A's shares are dematerialised and listed, the same shareholder calls a broker, places an order during trading hours and sees the price published each day.

lessons.tip: Before advising on any listed share, check ESX's latest notices and the company's own announcements; the market is changing month by month.

lessons.title: Capstone: Meskerem from placement to trading
body: Put the whole course together by following Meskerem one last time. For each step below, name the institution and what it does. Then check your answers against the lessons in Module 4.

Meskerem's story ends where a listed company's life begins: shares trade every day, investors watch its results, and the company must keep disclosing. In the next stage it plans a Birr 200 million bond on the Fixed Income Market, and a credit rating agency will grade it first.

items.text: Founded as a PLC by five founders; finance from bank loans and reinvested profit
Converts to a share company under the Commercial Code
Private placement of Birr 150 million to 35 investors
Entoto Capital appointed; prospectus filed with ECMA; shares dematerialised at the CSD
ECMA approves the offer; Birr 600 million raised; ESX lists the shares on the Growth Board

items.label: After listing
items.text: Brokers trade the shares on ESX; the CSD settles; ECMA supervises disclosure

scenario.title: The first trading day
scenario.situation: On Meskerem's first trading day, retail investor Hirut Alemayehu places an order through Sheba Securities to buy 300 shares. The order matches a sell order from a private placement investor at Birr 262.
scenario.question: Which institutions handle this trade, in order?
options: ECMA matches the order and the NBE records it
Meskerem matches the order and updates its paper register
Entoto Capital buys the shares and resells them to Hirut
Sheba Securities sends the order to ESX, ESX matches it in the order book, and the CSD transfers the shares to Hirut's account; ECMA supervises the whole process
scenario.explain: The broker routes the order, the exchange matches it, and the depository records the change of ownership, all under ECMA's supervision. The company no longer keeps a paper register for listed shares, and the investment bank's role ended with the offer.

takeaways: Retail, diaspora, institutional and foreign investors have different needs; foreign portfolio rules were still in draft as of September 2026
Investors weigh return, risk, liquidity and real return; monetary policy and FX reform move all of them
Private placements reach a limited number of selected investors; a public offer needs an ECMA-approved prospectus
The market's biggest pipeline is the base of unlisted share companies, especially banks and insurers, while liquidity is still low
A company's journey runs from share company conversion through placement, prospectus, dematerialisation and listing to daily trading

quiz.q: Which investors typically have long-term liabilities that suit long-term securities?
quiz.explain: Pension funds and insurers owe benefits years ahead, so long-term assets match them.

quiz.q: A bond yields 12% when inflation is 14%. The real return is roughly:
quiz.explain: Real return is about 12 minus 14, or minus 2 points.

quiz.q: What instrument was ECMA consulting on in September 2026 for foreign investors?
options: A draft Foreign Portfolio Investment Regulation
quiz.explain: ECMA posted a draft Foreign Portfolio Investment Regulation on 29 September 2026.

quiz.q: What usually happens to T-bill yields when the NBE raises the National Bank Rate?
quiz.explain: A higher policy rate pushes short-term yields up.

quiz.q: What is the largest untapped pool of potential listings in Ethiopia?
options: Unlisted share companies, especially banks and insurers
quiz.explain: Thousands of shareholders already hold shares in unlisted banks and insurers.

quiz.q: An offer of shares to several hundred members of the public without a prospectus is:
options: Allowed if the company is profitable
A public offer that needs ECMA approval
quiz.explain: Offering widely to the public needs an approved prospectus, whatever the company calls it.

simulation.title: A month as capital markets associate at Bank A Capital
setting: You have just joined Bank A Capital S.C., the ECMA-licensed investment bank subsidiary of Bank A, as an associate on its client desk in Addis Ababa. The desk is the first stop for everyone who wants to use the new market: Bank A branch customers who want to buy shares or bills, companies thinking about raising money, institutions with cash to place, and Bank A head office teams planning their own capital market business.

Bank A Capital advises issuers, arranges and underwrites offers, and reaches ESX through a licensed trading member arm. The market is young: ESX opened on 10 January 2025, liquidity is still low and many clients are buying a security for the first time. Your job is to give each of them a clear, correct answer, point them to the right instrument and the right institution, and build business the firm can be proud of.

You report to the head of the client desk, Ato Bereket Haile. This month he expects a full pipeline, zero compliance surprises and clients who understand what they bought. Items arrive in the order below, and some of your answers will come back to you later in the month.

authority.title: Your desk's rules and reference points

rows.label: ESX trading
rows.value: 9:00 to 15:00 after a 30-minute pre-open; lot size one share (ESX Rulebook, December 2024)

rows.label: Settlement cycle, tick size, price limits
rows.value: Not stated in the Rulebook; quote only from the latest CSD rules and ESX notices

rows.label: Costs of a share trade
rows.value: ECMA transaction fee 0.15% (Directive No. 996/2024); desk commission 0.5% (Bank A Capital's own rate)

rows.label: ECMA fee on a public share offer
rows.value: Birr 300,000 fixed plus 0.1% of the offer value (Directive No. 996/2024)

rows.label: Private placement
rows.value: No more than 100 investors, as reported under the public offer directive; more is a public offer needing an approved prospectus

rows.label: Who does what
rows.value: ECMA licenses and approves offers; ESX lists and matches; the CSD records ownership; the NBE runs T-bill auctions and approves bank investments (SBB/92/2024)

rows.label: Foreign portfolio investors
rows.value: Draft regulation posted for consultation on 29 September 2026; check the rules in force with compliance before onboarding

rows.label: Advice
rows.value: Suitability first: the client's needs, horizon and risk before any product

authority.note: These follow the course and current ECMA, ESX and NBE texts as the course reports them. Your own institution's policy always comes first, and fee and rate figures must be checked against the latest official notices.

meters.label: Advice quality
meters.help: Rises when you match the right instrument and institution to the need; falls with wrong facts or wrong products.

meters.label: Client trust
meters.help: Rises when clients get clear, honest and timely answers; falls with surprises, losses they did not understand or needless refusals.

meters.label: Compliance
meters.help: Falls sharply with any breach of ECMA, ESX or NBE rules, or a promise the rules do not support.

meters.label: Business pipeline
meters.help: Rises with sound mandates, trades and new clients; falls when good business is lost or a bad deal costs the firm.

tasks.from: Relationship manager, Bank A Hawassa branch
tasks.subject: Sidama Coffee Roasters PLC: Birr 25 million now and Birr 450 million later
body: Sidama Coffee Roasters PLC, a private limited company and a strong branch customer, needs Birr 25 million for four months to buy green coffee for a confirmed export order. Separately, the owners plan a Birr 450 million roasting and packaging plant over the next three years.
The owners asked the branch for one big 7-year loan for everything. The RM thinks the plant is too big for the branch and asks what Bank A Capital can offer. You run the numbers the owners sent.

exhibit.title: Sidama's plant financed fully by a bank loan (Birr millions, illustrative)

rows.label: Expected operating profit (EBIT), first full year

tasks.ask: What do you recommend to the RM?

options.text: Keep the coffee purchase as a short branch facility. For the plant, cover is only about 1.24 times (95 / 76.5), so propose a market finance study, starting with conversion to a share company.
options.outcome: Right match. Short, self-liquidating needs suit bank facilities; a large long-term plant is what capital markets are for, and equity carries no fixed charge in a bad year. Only a share company can offer shares to the public under the Commercial Code, so conversion comes first.

options.text: Propose one public share offer of about Birr 475 million to cover both the coffee purchase and the plant, so the owners raise everything in one process and avoid paying bank interest altogether.
options.outcome: A public offer takes months of preparation and ECMA review, so it cannot fund a coffee purchase due in four months. Match the source to the need: short money for short needs, long money for long ones.

options.text: Support the single 7-year loan of Birr 475 million: interest cover above 1.0 shows the company can pay, the owners know the business, and the branch keeps a strong customer on its books.
options.outcome: Cover of about 1.24 times (95 / 76.5) leaves almost no cushion if sales dip, and the plant must still be repaid on schedule whatever happens. Module 1 shows why large long-term projects often need equity alongside debt.

options.text: Tell the RM the company can list its shares on the ESX Growth Board next month as it is, since it is profitable and growing; Bank A Capital will prepare the documents quickly.
options.outcome: A private limited company cannot offer shares to the public; it must first convert to a share company, prepare audited accounts and an ECMA-approved prospectus. Promising a listing next month sets the client up for disappointment.

tasks.subject: Buying 2,000 shares at Birr 300: what will it cost, and when are they mine?
body: W/ro Meseret, a school director and a first-time investor, wants to buy 2,000 shares of a listed company at Birr 300 each. She has exactly Birr 605,000 in her Bank A account and must pay a builder on Thursday from what is left.
She asks two questions: how much will leave her account in total, and on what day the shares will settle. A colleague says, "Just tell her T+2, that is the norm everywhere."

exhibit.title: Her order and the charges (both fees on the buyer, per her agreement)

options.text: Total Birr 603,900 (600,000 plus 900 ECMA fee plus 3,000 commission), leaving her Birr 1,100. I will confirm the settlement date from the current CSD rules before she plans Thursday.
options.outcome: Correct: 600,000 x 0.15% = 900 and 600,000 x 0.5% = 3,000. The ESX Rulebook does not state a settlement cycle, so you quote it only from the latest CSD rules and ESX notices, not from another country's market.

options.text: Total Birr 603,900: Birr 600,000 for the shares, Birr 900 ECMA fee and Birr 3,000 commission. The shares settle T+2, as on most exchanges, so her Thursday payment is safe.
options.outcome: The arithmetic is right but the settlement promise is not yours to make. The Rulebook gives no settlement cycle, and a client who plans a payment around an assumed date can be hurt if it is wrong.

options.text: Total Birr 600,900: Birr 600,000 for the shares plus the Birr 900 ECMA fee. The commission is small, so I leave it out to keep her first trade simple, and settlement is usually quick.
options.outcome: Leaving out the Birr 3,000 commission understates her cost and may leave her short for the builder. Every charge that falls on the client belongs in the quote.

options.text: Advise her to wait: with Birr 605,000 in the account she is too close to the limit once fees are added, and a first-time investor should not buy until she has a bigger cash cushion.
options.outcome: She can afford it: the total is Birr 603,900. Your job is to give her the full cost and the facts she needs, then let her decide; the lot size of one share also lets her buy fewer if she wants a bigger cash buffer.

tasks.from: Ato Fikru Tolossa, shareholder of an unlisted insurer
tasks.subject: Please sell my 5,000 insurance shares on ESX this week
body: Ato Fikru holds 5,000 shares of a private insurance company that is not listed on ESX. Until now he could only sell through friends and then ask the company to record the transfer. He has a buyer's offer passed to him by a cousin, but he would rather "use the exchange".
He asks you to put his shares into the ESX order book this week. Your trading colleague says there is a gap in the order book for some insurance names and "nobody will check".

options.text: Explain that only listed shares trade in the ESX order book. His shares can trade over the counter through a licensed dealer under ECMA's OTC directive, or after a listing; offer to check the OTC route.
options.outcome: Right. Is the security listed, and did the order go to the exchange's order book? If not, it is OTC, which in Ethiopia sits under ECMA's directive (reported as No. 1009/2024). He gets a real path and an honest answer.

options.text: Enter the order under a similar listed insurance name, since the price is close, then ask the insurer's share registrar to record the transfer afterwards so Ato Fikru gets his money this week.
options.outcome: This is a serious breach: an unlisted security cannot be traded on ESX, and booking it under another name misleads the market and the buyer. Nothing excuses entering a false order.

options.text: Tell him to complete the private sale through his cousin's buyer, since that is how insurance shares have always changed hands, and ask the insurer's secretary to record the transfer in the register.
options.outcome: Private transfers are still possible, but you missed the chance to explain the regulated OTC route and the listing pipeline. The market exists to replace slow, opaque private deals with visible prices.

options.text: Decline politely: the desk deals only in ESX-listed shares, so he should keep his insurance shares until the company lists or he finds a buyer himself through his own contacts.
options.outcome: Correct on ESX, but a client-first desk explains the OTC option and the insurer's possible listing instead of closing the door. Many unlisted share companies are preparing to list, and he is a future client.

tasks.subject: Can I buy coffee futures on ESX to lock next season's price?
body: Ato Abdella exports washed coffee and worries that world prices may fall before next season. A friend told him that "ESX now has futures" and he wants to buy them through Bank A Capital today.
He is a large Bank A customer, and the branch manager has asked you to "say yes to whatever he needs".

options.text: Explain that ESX lists shares and bonds, not futures; derivatives exchanges may be licensed later, and ECX trades physical coffee. Bring in Bank A's trade and treasury teams on the tools available today.
options.outcome: Accurate and helpful. Derivatives are a future step in Ethiopia's framework; ECX is a physical commodity exchange, and bank FX products under NBE rules are separate. He leaves with the facts and a next step.

options.text: Say yes, and promise to find him a coffee futures contract on the ESX Growth Board this week, since the branch manager wants every need of this large customer met and he is ready to trade today.
options.outcome: There are no coffee futures on ESX. The Growth Board lists shares of smaller, younger companies. A promise the market cannot keep damages trust the moment he discovers it.

options.text: Tell him derivatives are banned in Ethiopia under the capital market law, so he must accept the price risk on next season's coffee, and suggest he simply hold back part of his stock instead.
options.outcome: Not true: the framework provides for derivatives exchanges to be licensed by ECMA. They are a later stage of development, not banned forever.

options.text: Suggest he buy coffee futures through the Ethiopia Commodity Exchange instead, since ECX is where coffee is traded, and offer to introduce him to an ECX member firm this afternoon.
options.outcome: ECX trades physical commodities such as coffee, sesame and pulses, not futures. Confusing the two is a common mistake that Module 3 warns against.

tasks.from: Trustee, Kombolcha Textile Employees' Provident Fund
tasks.subject: Birr 40 million of benefits due in 91 days: where should it sit?
body: The fund must pay Birr 40 million of retirement benefits in exactly 91 days. The trustee is considering three uses: the 91-day T-bill, a five-year corporate bond with a higher coupon, or listed bank shares that "everyone says will rise".
The latest 91-day T-bill yield is 11.0%, as reported by the NBE in July 2026. The trustee asks how much the fund would pay today to receive Birr 40 million at maturity.

options.text: Bid for Birr 40 million face of 91-day bills: at 11.0% the price is about Birr 38.93 million, and they repay exactly when the benefits fall due. I will confirm the auction basis.
options.outcome: Correct: 40,000,000 / (1 + 0.11 x 91 / 365) = 40,000,000 / 1.027425 = Birr 38,932,295, a gain of about Birr 1.07 million. Money needed on a known date belongs in a short, low-risk instrument that matures on that date.

options.text: Bid for Birr 40 million face of 91-day T-bills at a price of Birr 35.6 million (Birr 40 million less the 11% yield), which matures exactly when the benefits fall due.
options.outcome: That applies a full year's yield to a 91-day bill. The yield must be scaled by 91 / 365, which gives a price of about Birr 38.93 million. A wrong bid price can lose the auction or overpay.

options.text: Put it in the five-year corporate bond for its higher coupon and sell it in three months, so the fund earns more than the T-bill while it waits and still has cash on the payment date.
options.outcome: A long bond may be worth less when the benefits fall due, and with low liquidity it may be hard to sell at all. Matching the maturity to the payment date is the rule, not chasing the coupon.

options.text: Split it: Birr 20 million in 91-day T-bills to cover most of the payment, and Birr 20 million in listed bank shares for growth, since bank shares have paid good dividends.
options.outcome: Growth is the wrong goal for money already promised to retirees in three months. Shares can fall, and the fund could be short on the payment date.

tasks.from: Strategy officer, Bank A head office
tasks.subject: Board paper on a new Bank A asset management subsidiary: please check by tonight
body: Head office is preparing a board paper on setting up a second subsidiary, an asset management company. The draft says: "ECMA will approve Bank A's equity investment in the subsidiary, and the NBE will license it as a fund manager. Once licensed, the subsidiary will trade directly on ESX for its funds without a broker."
The strategy officer says the paper goes to the board tomorrow morning and asks only for "a quick thumbs up".

options.text: Correct it: the NBE approves the investment under SBB/92/2024; ECMA licenses the fund manager under Directive No. 980/2024; funds reach ESX through a member, with an independent custodian.
options.outcome: Right on every point. Bank investments are an NBE prudential matter, licensing is ECMA's job, investors reach ESX through members, and collective scheme assets sit with an independent custodian, not the manager.

options.text: Give the thumbs up tonight so the paper reaches the board on time: the regulators will tell Bank A what they need during the application, and the board can sort out the details at the next meeting.
options.outcome: A board approving a paper that sends the wrong application to the wrong regulator wastes months and looks careless to both the NBE and ECMA. A quick check is exactly when errors like this must be caught.

options.text: Swap the two regulators, so the NBE approves the investment and ECMA licenses the fund manager, but leave the rest of the paper as it is, including direct ESX trading by the new subsidiary.
options.outcome: Half right. The regulators are now correct, but the paper still says the subsidiary will trade on ESX without a member and is silent on the custodian, both points a careful board would challenge.

options.text: Reply that ESX licenses fund managers and approves bank investments in them, so the paper should name ESX for both approvals and drop the references to ECMA and the NBE.
options.outcome: ESX admits members and lists securities but does not license firms. ECMA licenses all capital market service providers under Directive No. 980/2024.

tasks.subject: A first public offer: which board, and what will ECMA charge?
body: Rift Solar Energy S.C. is a five-year-old solar installer growing fast, with three years of audited accounts. It plans to offer 2 million new shares at Birr 150. The CFO wants to know which ESX market fits and has budgeted "about Birr 600,000 for the whole offer, since that is the ECMA fee".
He also wants Bank A Capital to quote for the mandate this week.

rows.label: ECMA fee on a share offer
rows.value: Birr 300,000 fixed plus 0.1% of offer value

rows.label: Company profile
rows.value: 5 years old, fast growth, short record

tasks.ask: What do you tell the CFO?

options.text: The offer is Birr 300 million, so the ECMA fee is Birr 600,000, about 0.2% of the money raised; adviser, legal, audit and marketing costs come on top. The Growth Board looks the likely fit.
options.outcome: Correct: 2 million x Birr 150 = Birr 300 million; 0.1% is Birr 300,000; plus the Birr 300,000 fixed fee gives Birr 600,000. The regulator's fee is only part of the cost, and a younger, fast-growing issuer usually suits the Growth Board.

options.text: Confirm his Birr 600,000 budget: that is the full ECMA fee on a Birr 300 million offer, and it covers the regulator. Recommend the Main Board, which gives a new issuer more prestige with investors.
options.outcome: The fee figure is right, but it is not the cost of the whole offer, and the Main Board is for larger, established companies meeting full listing requirements. Both errors will surface painfully later in the process.

options.text: The ECMA fee is Birr 300,000 only, since the 0.1% variable part applies to offers above Birr 1 billion. That leaves him Birr 300,000 of his budget for advisers. The Growth Board fits.
options.outcome: There is no such threshold in the fee rule as the course reports it: the 0.1% applies to the full offer value, giving Birr 600,000 in total.

options.text: Suggest the Fixed Income Market, which has lighter listing rules for young companies than either equity board, and confirm the ECMA fee of Birr 600,000 as the main cost to budget.
options.outcome: The Fixed Income Market lists bonds and other debt securities, not shares. A share offer for a young company points to the Growth Board.

tasks.from: Head of equity capital markets, Bank A Capital
tasks.subject: Offer closed undersubscribed: what do we fund tomorrow?
body: Bank A Capital fully underwrote a Birr 300 million share offer for a fictional client, Tana Foods S.C.: 2 million shares at Birr 150. The offer closed today. Valid applications came in for 1.7 million shares.
Finance needs the amount Bank A Capital must pay by tomorrow, and the client's CFO is asking how much Tana Foods will receive.

rows.label: Shares applied for by the public
Underwriting
rows.value: Firm, for the full offer, at the offer price

options.text: We buy the 300,000 untaken shares for Birr 45 million at the offer price. Tana Foods receives the full Birr 300 million before costs. We sell the shares over time.
options.outcome: Correct: 2,000,000 minus 1,700,000 = 300,000 shares x Birr 150 = Birr 45 million. Underwriting shifts the risk of a failed offer to the investment bank, which is why investment banks need far more capital than advisers.

options.text: Tana Foods receives the Birr 255 million the public paid. Our underwriting fee is still due, and we tell the CFO the shortfall reflects market demand, not our commitment.
options.outcome: Under a firm underwriting the issuer gets the full amount. Walking away from the commitment breaks the agreement and the market's trust in Bank A Capital's word.

options.text: Ask the public applicants to take up the extra 300,000 shares pro rata before we fund anything, since they already wanted the company and this keeps our capital free.
options.outcome: Applicants bought what they chose; the underwriter cannot push its commitment onto them. Bank A Capital must fund Birr 45 million tomorrow.

options.text: We must fund Birr 255 million tomorrow, the amount the public applied for, and Tana Foods receives Birr 300 million; finance should move the cash from our T-bills today.
options.outcome: The public's Birr 255 million comes from the applicants. The underwriter pays only for the shortfall: 300,000 shares, Birr 45 million.

tasks.subject: A quick private placement to 320 people on Telegram
body: Gondar Dairy Farms S.C., a share company, wants to raise Birr 60 million. The founder plans to invite 320 customers, suppliers and neighbors through a Telegram group to buy shares at Birr 500, without a prospectus. "It is just a private placement among friends," he says.
He offers Bank A Capital a fee of Birr 1.2 million to "handle the paperwork" and wants to start Monday. Your desk head reminds you the month's fee target is still short.

options.text: An offer to 320 people is above the reported 100-investor limit, so it is a public offer needing an ECMA-approved prospectus. Offer a true placement to 100 or fewer, or a proper public offer.
options.outcome: Right. Who is protected decides the route: a public offer reaches anyone, so it needs an approved prospectus. You keep the client and the fee opportunity on a lawful basis.

options.text: Take the mandate as described and start Monday: friends, customers and suppliers know the farm and can assess it themselves, and the Birr 1.2 million fee closes this month's gap.
options.outcome: Calling it private does not change the rule. An offer to hundreds of people without a prospectus breaches the public offer directive, and Bank A Capital would be the licensed firm that handled it.

options.text: Agree, as long as the shares are never listed on ESX: an unlisted share company selling to its own community is a private matter, so no prospectus is needed and we can start Monday.
options.outcome: Listing is a separate question. A public offer needs an approved prospectus whether or not the shares are later listed.

options.text: Decline and end the call: Bank A Capital does not deal with small issuers, and a Birr 60 million raise is not worth the desk's time when larger mandates are in the pipeline.
options.outcome: You avoided the breach but lost a client who needed advice. Explaining the lawful routes is both compliant and good business.

tasks.from: Ato Mulugeta Assefa, retired civil engineer
tasks.subject: Put my Birr 2 million into the newest listing
body: Ato Mulugeta, 67, sold his house and has Birr 2 million. He needs about Birr 15,000 a month to live on and has no pension. Friends made money on a recent listing, and he wants all of it in one newly listed share tomorrow.
The commission on Birr 2 million would be Birr 10,000, a good start to your monthly target. He is impatient and says, "It is my money, just do it."

options.text: Explain the risk of one new share. Keep a year or two of living costs in T-bills or deposits, put only money he can leave for years into diversified shares or a fund, and record his decision.
options.outcome: Suitability comes first. A retiree who depends on the money needs liquidity and safety before growth, and concentration in one new share puts his living costs at risk.

options.text: Do as he asks and buy the new listing tomorrow: it is his money and his written instruction, the commission helps the desk's target, and he has heard good things from his friends.
options.outcome: Executing a clearly unsuitable plan without explaining the risk fails the duty to advise. When the price moves against him, he will remember who said nothing.

options.text: Tell him shares always beat T-bills over time, so putting the Birr 2 million into the new listing is a sound long-term plan, and he can sell a few shares each month for living costs.
options.outcome: No investment is always better. Saying so is misleading advice, and it ignores his need for monthly income.

options.text: Refuse the order: retirees with no pension should not hold shares at all, so tell him to keep the full Birr 2 million in a savings deposit at the branch.
options.outcome: Refusing service is not the answer. A small, diversified share holding can suit a retiree once his income needs are safe.

tasks.from: Diaspora client, by email from Toronto
tasks.subject: Is 11% on T-bills a real gain for my family's savings?
body: Ato Samuel Bekele, a long-standing diaspora client, plans to keep Birr 3 million in rolling 91-day T-bills for ten years to build his children's education fund. He asks whether the 11.0% yield means his savings will grow in real terms.
The latest NBE figures reported in July 2026: 91-day T-bill yield 11.0%, headline inflation 13.4% (May 2026).

options.text: The real return is about minus 2.1% (1.110 / 1.134 minus 1), so T-bills alone lose buying power. For a ten-year goal, discuss a diversified mix including shares or a fund.
options.outcome: Correct: 1.110 / 1.134 = 0.9788, a real return of about minus 2.1%. Investors weigh return, risk, liquidity and real return; a long horizon can carry more risk, but no outcome is guaranteed.

options.text: Yes: 11% is a strong real gain, well above most deposit rates, and rolling 91-day bills for ten years keeps his Birr 3 million safe while it grows for the children's education.
options.outcome: The real return is what matters for buying power, and at 13.4% inflation it is negative. Confusing nominal and real return is a basic error with real costs over ten years.

options.text: The real return is plus 2.4% (13.4 minus 11.0), so rolling T-bills for ten years will grow the fund in real terms with almost no risk; I recommend he keeps the plan as it is.
options.outcome: The sign is wrong: 11.0 minus 13.4 is minus 2.4 points (about minus 2.1% exactly). Check the arithmetic before advising.

options.text: Move the full Birr 3 million into listed bank shares now, since T-bills lose money after inflation and bank shares have paid high dividends; review it again in ten years.
options.outcome: Swinging from all bills to all shares ignores risk and diversification. Real return is one input; the plan should balance it with risk and liquidity.

tasks.from: Portfolio manager, a Nairobi-based fund manager
tasks.subject: We want to buy USD 2 million of ESX-listed bank shares next week
body: A foreign fund manager with no Ethiopian ties wants to open an account and buy listed bank shares worth about USD 2 million next week. It has read that "foreign investors are now welcome".
Your desk head is excited: it would be the desk's largest client. ECMA posted a draft Foreign Portfolio Investment Regulation for consultation on 29 September 2026.

options.text: Welcome the interest, explain that the foreign portfolio rules are a draft posted on 29 September 2026, and confirm with compliance which rules apply before any onboarding.
options.outcome: Right balance. Foreign investors are a growing source of demand, but until the regulation is adopted you check the rules in force before advising or onboarding. You keep the relationship warm without overpromising.

options.text: Open the account and execute next week: the draft regulation shows the direction of travel, the fund is a regulated manager, and we would win the desk's largest client before competitors do.
options.outcome: A draft is not a rule in force. Acting on it before adoption exposes the client and Bank A Capital to a breach and possible reversal of the trades.

options.text: Reply that foreign investors can never buy Ethiopian listed shares under current law, so there is no point opening an account, and thank them for their interest in the market.
options.outcome: Too absolute. The draft regulation is expected to set the terms on which foreign investors may buy listed securities. Closing the door loses a future client.

options.text: Suggest they buy through an Ethiopian relative's or partner's account in the meantime, then move the holding into their own name once the foreign portfolio regulation is final.
options.outcome: Using a nominee to get around investor rules defeats identity checks and investor eligibility. A licensed firm must never suggest it.

followUps.subject: You said T+2, but my shares are not settled and my builder is waiting
body: W/ro Meseret planned her builder payment around the T+2 settlement you quoted. The trade has not yet settled under the current CSD timetable, and she believes something has gone wrong with her money. She is upset and has told two friends who were about to open accounts.

options.text: Apologize, confirm the actual date from the CSD rules, show her that her cash and order are safe, and log the error with your desk head.
options.outcome: Honest repair. The lesson from Module 2: settlement cycle, tick size and price limits are not in the Rulebook, so quote only from the latest official notice.

options.text: Tell her delays are normal in a young market and she should be patient; explain that T+2 is the usual cycle and that the CSD will settle her trade as soon as it can.
options.outcome: It shifts the blame for your own wrong quote. She needs the correct date and an apology, not a lecture on the market.

options.text: Offer to lend her the builder's payment from your own pocket until the trade settles, so she does not file a complaint and the desk's record stays clean this month.
options.outcome: Personal financial dealings with a client create a conflict and hide the error from your firm. Report it and fix it through the proper channel.

followUps.subject: ECMA inquiry: unregistered offer by Gondar Dairy Farms
body: ECMA has written to Bank A Capital asking for all documents on the Gondar Dairy Farms share sale. Investors in the Telegram group complained that they received no prospectus and cannot find audited accounts. The founder says Bank A Capital told him the offer was fine.

options.text: Give compliance every document and message, cooperate fully with ECMA, and support a remedy for investors, such as a prospectus and an offer of refunds.
options.outcome: Full cooperation and a remedy for investors are the only sound path. The lesson stands: a public offer needs an approved prospectus, whatever the issuer calls it.

options.text: Tell compliance the founder misunderstood the call and that the desk gave no advice, since no engagement letter was signed and the fee was never invoiced.
options.outcome: Misleading your own compliance team and the regulator turns a breach into a far more serious conduct failure. Records will show what was said.

options.text: Hand over the file to compliance but refuse any remedy for investors, since the founder has already spent the money on cows and the firm never received its fee.
options.outcome: Cooperation is required, but investor protection is the reason the rule exists. Working toward a remedy is part of putting it right.

followUps.subject: The share fell 30% and I cannot pay my rent
body: The newly listed share fell from its first-day price after weak half-year results. Ato Mulugeta's Birr 2 million is now worth about Birr 1.4 million. Trading is thin, and to cover three months of living costs he has to sell into a falling market. He asks what he should do and says he was never told the risks.

options.text: Escalate to your desk head and compliance, sell only what he needs for living costs in an orderly way, and rebuild his plan with a cash and T-bill reserve.
options.outcome: Escalating and fixing the plan is the right recovery. The original lesson is that suitability comes before the trade: liquidity and safety first for money a client lives on.

options.text: Advise him to buy more at the lower price to average down, so that a recovery brings him back to Birr 2 million faster, and to borrow for the rent in the meantime.
options.outcome: Doubling the concentration in a client who cannot pay his rent compounds the original unsuitable advice.

options.text: Tell him the decision was his, show him his signed order for the full Birr 2 million, and close the meeting without logging a complaint.
options.outcome: The instruction was his, but the duty to explain the risk was yours. Walking away invites a complaint the firm will struggle to defend.

memo.prompt: Write your end-of-month hand-over note to the head of the client desk.
guide: The two client answers you are most confident in, and the rule or calculation behind each.
Any answer you would correct, and what you have done to put it right.
Mandates and leads in the pipeline, with the next step and date for each.
One market fact the desk must check against a fresh official notice before quoting it to clients.

exam.q: Meskerem needs Birr 600 million for a plant that will take years to pay back. Expected EBIT is Birr 120 million and a loan would cost Birr 102 million in year-1 interest. What does this suggest?
options: A loan is clearly best because interest is tax deductible
Meskerem should use a three-month overdraft
Interest coverage of about 1.2 times leaves little cushion, so equity or a mix with equity is worth considering
exam.explain: 120 / 102 is about 1.18 times, a thin margin; equity has no fixed charge.

exam.q: Which statement about Ethiopia's capital market history is accurate?
options: An informal share dealing group operated in Addis Ababa in the 1960s, and organised trading resumed only with ESX in 2025
ESX has operated continuously since the 1960s
exam.explain: The 1960s group ended with nationalisation; the 2021 proclamation created ECMA and ESX launched in 2025.

exam.q: Mekdes sells 400 Meskerem shares on ESX at Birr 300. How much new capital does Meskerem receive from this trade?
exam.explain: A secondary market trade transfers money between investors only.

exam.q: A bank invests surplus funds for 91 days. Which market and instrument fit?
exam.explain: Short-term liquidity belongs in the money market, for example a 91-day T-bill.

exam.q: Shares of an unlisted insurer are traded through a licensed dealer between two parties. Which rules govern this market?
options: ECMA's directive on exchanges, derivatives exchanges and the OTC market
The ESX Rulebook's Main Board rules
exam.explain: The OTC market sits under the ECMA directive, not the Rulebook.

exam.q: Which of these is set out in the ESX Rulebook (December 2024)?
options: Trading from 9:00 to 15:00 with a 30-minute pre-open
exam.explain: The Rulebook sets trading hours and pre-open; it states no settlement cycle or price limits, and the lot is one share.

exam.q: An investor buys 2,000 shares at Birr 150. What is the ECMA transaction fee at 0.15%?
Using the simple formula, what is the price of a Birr 100,000, 91-day T-bill at an 11.0% yield?
A share bought at Birr 240 pays a Birr 18 dividend and ends the year at Birr 228. What is the total return before costs?
exam.explain: Dividend 18 plus price change minus 12 is 6; 6 / 240 = 2.5%.

exam.q: Why does a corporate bond normally yield more than a government bond of the same term?
options: Investors demand a credit spread for the risk that the company cannot pay
ECMA sets corporate yields higher by rule
exam.explain: The extra yield compensates for the issuer's credit risk.

exam.q: Under NBE Proclamation No. 1359/2025, how may the NBE support government borrowing?
options: By buying any amount of new government bonds at auction
Through a limited overdraft, but not by buying government securities in the primary market
exam.explain: Article 27 caps the overdraft and bars primary-market purchases of government securities.

exam.q: A coffee exporter wants to hedge next season's price on ESX. What is accurate?
options: ESX lists coffee futures on the Growth Board
Derivatives exchanges can be licensed under ECMA's framework, but exchange-traded derivatives are a future step; ECX trades physical commodities
exam.explain: ESX lists shares and debt; ECX trades physical commodities; derivatives are still to come.

exam.q: In a unit trust, which arrangement protects investors if the fund manager fails?
options: An independent custodian holds the fund's assets separately
The manager keeps the assets in its own account
exam.explain: Separation of custody from management protects unit holders.

exam.q: A firm wants to execute client orders on ESX for a commission. Which licence and body apply?
options: A dealer licence from the NBE
A broker licence from ECMA, and ESX membership
exam.explain: ECMA licenses brokers under Directive No. 980/2024; ESX admits them as members.

exam.q: What is the minimum capital range across ECMA's licence categories under Directive No. 980/2024?
exam.explain: It runs from Birr 100,000 (individual adviser) to Birr 100 million (bank-group investment bank or custodian).

exam.q: A company offers Birr 200 million of new shares. Using the ECMA share offer fee of Birr 300,000 plus 0.1%, what is the fee?
Put these steps of a listing in order: (1) ESX admits shares, (2) conversion to a share company, (3) ECMA approves the prospectus, (4) CSD dematerialises shares.
exam.explain: A company first converts, then gets its offer approved, has its shares dematerialised and finally is admitted to trading.

exam.q: A pension fund must pay benefits in three months. A T-bill yields 11% and inflation is 13.4%. What is the best judgment?
options: Hold the T-bill: it matches the payment date, even though its real return is slightly negative
Move the money into one listed share to beat inflation
exam.explain: Matching the payment date and protecting capital comes first for a known short-term liability.

exam.q: Rift Valley Solar invites 450 people through social media to buy shares without a prospectus. Under the reported private placement limit, this is:
options: A private placement, since no listing is planned
An OTC transaction needing NBE approval
Allowed for companies under five years old
A public offer needing ECMA approval
exam.explain: An offer to more than the reported 100-investor limit is a public offer that needs an approved prospectus.

exam.q: Which development would most directly increase liquidity on ESX?
options: More listings of widely held share companies, such as banks and insurers, and more active institutional investors
exam.explain: More securities and more active investors raise trading volumes; the other options reduce them.
